issues.subcategory: unsupported extrapolation to untested population
issues.description: A sentence claiming that findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings appears mid-paragraph, completely unsupported by any data in the manuscript. The study exclusively used sex-segregated chains (exclusively male or exclusively female), no mixed-gender condition was ever tested, and no citation or theoretical basis is provided for this claim. The sentence also disrupts the grammatical and logical flow of the surrounding paragraph (it is sandwiched between statements about unidimensional representations of object motion), strongly suggesting it is an erroneously inserted or fabricated sentence. This constitutes a critical unsubstantiated empirical claim.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: systematic error in speed calculation due to distance mismatch
issues.description: The manuscript states that wheel speed is calculated as '1m/descent time,' yet the Methods section specifies that the two push-button timing switches were located '92 cm apart on the rails,' not 1 meter. Using 1 m in the numerator when the actual timed distance is 0.92 m introduces a systematic overestimation of all reported speeds by approximately 8.7% (1/0.92 ≈ 1.087). Every speed value reported in the paper (e.g., 123.6 m/h, 145.7 m/h, maximum ~154 m/h) is therefore inflated. This also means the stated maximum speed of ~154 m/h and the 71% optimization claim are both computed from a systematically incorrect distance. The physical interpretations and comparisons remain directionally valid, but all absolute speed values are incorrect.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) ... Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails

issues.subcategory: mislabeling of Bayesian credible intervals as frequentist confidence intervals
issues.description: The Methods section explicitly states 'We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R... 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences,' yet throughout the Results section the same intervals are repeatedly labeled '95% Confidence Intervals' (abbreviated CI). Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals have fundamentally different interpretations: a 95% credible interval means there is a 95% posterior probability the parameter lies within the range, whereas a 95% confidence interval is a long-run frequency statement about the procedure. This mislabeling creates confusion about the inferential framework used and misrepresents the meaning of the reported intervals.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h ... Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52)

issues.subcategory: incorrect units for regression slope coefficients
issues.description: The reported 'mean' and credible intervals for the 'Generation' predictor are regression slope coefficients representing the change in wheel speed per generation (units: m/h per generation), yet they are presented with units of 'm/h' — the same unit used for speed itself. Similarly, the 'Treatment' coefficient and 'Generation x Treatment' interaction are reported as 'm/h' when they represent differences in speed intercepts and differences in slopes, respectively. This conflation of units makes it impossible to distinguish point estimates for raw speeds from rate-of-change coefficients, hampering interpretation and replication.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h ... Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.subcategory: post-hoc model selection without pre-specified criteria
issues.description: For Analysis 1 (the primary preregistered analysis of wheel speed), the authors selected the final model specification after comparing candidate models based on fit to observed data, without specifying in the pre-registration which model selection criterion would be used or which candidate models would be considered. This introduces undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom: the chosen model is the one that best fit the data, potentially capitalizing on chance. The pre-registration presumably specified a model structure; any deviation or selection procedure should be explicitly compared against what was pre-registered.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: undisclosed deviation from pre-registered analysis with post-hoc justification
issues.description: The pre-registered Analysis 4 (understanding across treatments) specified separate scores for inertia and centre-of-mass understanding as the outcome, with 'Physical Principle' and 'Physical Principle:Treatment' as predictors. The authors deviated by aggregating these two scores, justifying the deviation by claiming the pre-registered model 'did not converge.' However, convergence failure is often addressable through reparameterization, informative priors, or model simplification — it does not necessarily mandate aggregating conceptually distinct outcomes. Critically, the key exploratory findings (that inherited theory type differentially affects inertia vs. CoM understanding in opposite directions) are entirely invisible in the aggregated outcome used in Analysis 4. The deviation thus obscures the most theoretically interesting pattern, which is then reported only in post-hoc exploratory analyses without the same confirmatory status.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated...As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable 'Physical Principle' in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: absence of blinding for data collection and analysis
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that neither data collection nor data analysis was performed blind to experimental conditions. The experimenter, who manually positioned the weights on the physical wheel for every trial, knew which condition each participant was in. This creates potential for subtle experimenter effects (e.g., differential care, speed, or precision in placing weights) that could systematically bias performance outcomes between the 'Configurations' and 'Configurations + Theory' treatments. Additionally, non-blind analysis introduces risk of confirmation bias in decisions such as model selection, outlier handling, and interpretation of borderline results.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments... Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate imputation of zero speed for non-descending wheels
issues.description: For Analysis 3, wheels that did not descend were assigned a speed of 0. A non-descending wheel is physically a distinct failure event — it either remained stationary or rolled backward — and assigning speed=0 is an arbitrary placeholder that does not represent the actual outcome. This creates a severely bimodal outcome distribution (many zeros and a cluster around 100-160 m/h) that violates the normality assumption of the linear model. Furthermore, a speed of 0 implies the wheel was stationary for infinite time, which inflates the apparent variance and distorts the generation and treatment coefficients. The appropriate approach would be to model the two outcomes (descend vs. not descend) as a two-part (hurdle) model or use censored regression, and the rationale for the chosen approach should be pre-specified.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: contradictory handling of non-descending wheels across analyses
issues.description: Analysis 1 handles non-descending wheels by restricting data to trials where wheels descended ('Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset'), implying effective exclusion or at minimum de-emphasis of non-descending events. Analysis 3 handling the same outcome variable across treatments explicitly assigns speed=0 to all non-descending wheels. These two approaches are contradictory: exclusion and zero-imputation have fundamentally different statistical effects. A non-descending wheel removed from the sample is missing data; a non-descending wheel coded as 0 is an influential low-value observation. Using different strategies for the same type of event in different analyses without justification undermines the internal consistency of the statistical approach.
issues.quote: Analysis 1: 'Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.' Analysis 3: 'Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.'

issues.subcategory: causal claim from non-randomized exploratory association
issues.description: The paper presents a causal claim — 'the transmission of these inaccurate theories constrains learners' exploration and has downstream effects on their understanding' — as if it were experimentally established. However, participants in the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment were not randomly assigned to receive different theory types (inertia vs. centre-of-mass vs. full vs. irrelevant). The theory type inherited depended on what the previous participant wrote, which itself depended on their performance, exploration patterns, and prior beliefs — all potential confounders. The association between inherited theory type and subsequent exploration is observational and susceptible to confounding by initial chain tendencies, performance level, and other chain-level factors. The paper does conduct a secondary analysis using 'Configurations'-only participants grouped by exploration type, but this too is observational.
issues.quote: the transmission of these inaccurate theories constrains learners' exploration and has downstream effects on their understanding... Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass

issues.subcategory: critically underpowered subgroup with N=6
issues.description: The 'full theory' subgroup (participants who inherited a theory containing accurate information about both inertia and centre of mass) contains only N=6 participants. Heatmaps of exploration and comparison of understanding scores are presented for this group on equal visual footing with larger subgroups (N=15 inertia, N=17 CoM, N=18 irrelevant). No formal statistical test of differences between this N=6 group and others is reported, and visual heatmaps from 6 individuals are entirely unreliable for characterizing population-level exploration patterns. Any apparent 'finding' from this subgroup (e.g., 'The few participants who inherited a full theory produced compact and asymmetrical wheels') cannot be interpreted as a meaningful result due to extreme underpowering.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (Figure 3D and H).

issues.subcategory: absence of formal statistical tests for key exploratory comparisons
issues.description: The exploratory findings about differences in understanding scores between participants who inherited different theory types (Figure 3I) — described as one of the paper's three main findings — are presented with means and standard error bars but without formal statistical tests (e.g., no Bayesian model output, no credible intervals, no Bayes factors comparing groups). For the preregistered analyses, model outputs are provided in supplementary tables; for these exploratory analyses, only a figure with error bars is presented. This is insufficient for readers to evaluate whether the observed differences are reliable or attributable to sampling variation, particularly given the small and unequal subgroup sizes.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia theory reduces understanding about centre of mass and increases understanding about inertia, while inheriting a centre-of-mass theory increases understanding about centre of mass and reduces understanding about inertia (I).

issues.subcategory: no pre-test measure of causal understanding
issues.description: The understanding test is administered only after participants complete all 5 building trials, with no baseline pre-test measure. This design cannot distinguish between (a) what participants knew before the experiment, (b) what they learned during the 5 trials, and (c) whether the inherited social information (configurations or theories) changed their pre-existing understanding. The central claim — that 'participants' understanding did not improve across generations' — is specifically about between-generation comparisons of post-task scores, which is methodologically valid for that comparison. However, within-session learning is entirely uncharacterized, and the claim that 'most participants actually produced incorrect or incomplete theories despite the relative simplicity of the physical system' could partly reflect the limitations of post-task measurement rather than a true absence of learning.
issues.quote: Participants' understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels... after they completed their 5 trials.

issues.subcategory: prediction task may measure implicit intuition rather than explicit causal understanding
issues.description: The understanding measure requires participants to predict which of two wheels will be faster, with a monetary incentive for correct answers. Participants can achieve correct predictions through pattern recognition, perceptual similarity, or implicit intuitive physics — none of which constitute 'causal understanding' in the sense used throughout the paper's theoretical framing. The paper conflates predictive accuracy with causal understanding: a participant who correctly predicts that heavier outer weights slow a wheel may do so because it 'looks heavier' or through analogy to other objects, not because they understand moment of inertia as a causal mechanism. This is especially problematic given the paper's focus on the distinction between 'having a causal theory' and 'not having a causal theory,' since the measure cannot reliably distinguish these.
issues.quote: Participants' understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.subcategory: discrepancy between stated physical maximum speed and payoff formula maximum
issues.description: The paper states 'the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h,' yet the payoff formula uses MaxSpeed = 160. This inconsistency means the payoff formula is calibrated against a maximum that is physically unachievable, so the maximum possible per-wheel payoff is [1 - (160-154)/(160-96)] × 3 + 0.2 ≈ 2.92€, not the apparent maximum of 3.20€. While this does not fundamentally compromise the experimental incentive structure (relative differences in payoffs still reward improvement), the discrepancy suggests either that the physical maximum was not precisely determined before designing the payoff formula, or that the '154 m/h' maximum is itself an approximation with unclear provenance.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h... [1 - ((MaxSpeed – RecordedSpeed) / (MaxSpeed – MinSpeed))] x 3 + Bonus with MaxSpeed = 160

issues.subcategory: optimization percentage inconsistent with reported values
issues.description: The paper claims '71% optimization after only four cultural generations.' Using the paper's own reported values (Generation 1 speed = 123.6 m/h, Generation 5 speed = 145.7 m/h, maximum ≈ 154 m/h), the calculation is: (145.7 − 123.6) / (154 − 123.6) = 22.1 / 30.4 = 72.7%, not 71%. This discrepancy suggests either the optimization percentage was calculated from slightly different underlying values not reported in the main text, or there is an arithmetic error. While numerically minor, it reflects imprecision in reporting and is inconsistent with the stated values in the same paragraph.
issues.quote: these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: absence of statistical power analysis with inadequate justification
issues.description: The authors explicitly state that no methods were used to pre-determine sample size, justifying their choice solely by comparison with prior publications. This is insufficient for evaluating statistical power, particularly for the key null result (no treatment effect of theory transmission on wheel performance) and for the small subgroup analyses (N=6 to N=18). A post-hoc power analysis or equivalence test would be needed to determine whether the null results represent true absence of an effect or merely insufficient power to detect one. Reporting a null result ('the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution') as a substantive finding requires demonstrating that the study could have detected a meaningful effect if one existed.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD sample and student demographics not adequately acknowledged as limitation
issues.description: All participants were French university students recruited from Lille universities, an explicitly WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) sample. The paper's conclusions are framed in terms of human cultural evolution broadly and the evolution of technology in traditional societies (bows, kayaks, houses). While the paper briefly mentions future cross-cultural work as needed, it does not adequately acknowledge that French university students likely have formal physics and mathematics education that shapes both their intuitions and their theory formation, and that the results may not generalize to populations without formal schooling or with different folk physics traditions.
issues.quote: we asked successive 'cultural generations' of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system... our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities

issues.subcategory: extrapolation from low-dimensional task to high-dimensional real-world technologies
issues.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the wheel is a 'low-dimensional' optimization problem (2 variables: moment of inertia and centre of mass position) and describes this as a 'conservative test.' However, this framing is potentially backward: it may be easier to achieve cultural accumulation without understanding in a 2D space (where random exploration covers the space efficiently) than in high-dimensional spaces like bow construction where systematic causal reasoning might be necessary to navigate the fitness landscape. The main conclusions — that 'complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning' — are not directly supported by the low-dimensional paradigm used, and the authors do not provide theoretical or computational modeling to bridge this gap.
issues.quote: the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous timing of theory writing relative to understanding test
issues.description: The methods state that 'participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed,' implying the theory was written during the test phase (after the building phase ended). This creates ambiguity: (1) did participants write the theory before any test questions, partway through, or after all 10 questions? (2) Could viewing test questions (which showed pairs of wheels varying in inertia or CoM) have influenced the theory content? If theory writing occurred after some test questions, there is circularity: the test questions that measure understanding may have cued participants about relevant parameters, contaminating both the understanding measure and the theory content that is transmitted downstream.
issues.quote: In the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment, participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.subcategory: overclaiming null result as positive evidence of no effect
issues.description: Throughout the paper, the finding that theory transmission does not significantly change wheel performance is presented as positive evidence for the claim that 'the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.' In Bayesian terms, a credible interval that includes zero indicates uncertainty about the direction of an effect, not that the effect is zero. Without presenting Bayes factors comparing a null model against alternatives, or equivalence tests specifying a smallest effect size of interest, the null result cannot be interpreted as evidence of absence. The credible interval for the Treatment effect on speed (-10.76, 18.13) is wide and consistent with effects of considerable practical magnitude in either direction.
issues.quote: Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution... these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization

issues.subcategory: first-generation C+T participants' theories not accounted for in coding analysis
issues.description: The theory coding analysis describes '56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the Configurations + Theory treatment except first-generation participants),' categorizing them by theory type. However, the 14 first-generation participants in the C+T treatment also wrote and transmitted theories (to second-generation participants) but are not described in the coding analysis. Their theory distribution is relevant for understanding the origins of downstream theory inheritance effects and for characterizing what types of theories naive participants spontaneously generate versus what they inherit. The omission of these 14 theories from the coding results represents a gap in reporting.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of interpretation of Generation x Treatment interaction
issues.description: The paper reports the Generation × Treatment interaction for understanding scores as having a 95% CI of (0.03, 0.81) with mean = 0.44, and interprets this as meaning 'participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory.' A positive generation × treatment interaction means that the rate of increase in understanding per generation is steeper in the C+T treatment, not specifically that the last generation benefits most. This interpretation conflates a differential slope with a specific generational comparison. To test whether the last generation specifically has better understanding, a planned contrast comparing generation 5 across treatments would be required, which is not reported.
issues.quote: participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment 95% CI: (-2.54, 0.31), mean = -1.14; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44)
